title: The Blume-Capel Model as a $φ^6$ Field Theory: A Monte Carlo and Flow Model Study
authors: Ejaaz Merali, Ryan Larson, Ehsan Khatami, Richard T. Scalettar
abstract: We report Monte Carlo simulations of a continuous spin variant of the Blume-Capel model. We compute the phase diagrams in the crystal-field-temperature plane, as a function of the softness of the spins. We show that normalizing flows, a class of generative models capable of direct sampling without autocorrelation, are effective samplers across the phase diagram, including in the first-order transition region and in the vicinity of the tricritical point. Finite-size scaling analyses of flow samples locate the first- and second-order transitions as well as the tricritical point with accuracy comparable to canonical and extended-ensemble Monte Carlo.
summary: This work analyzes the Blume-Capel model by reformulating it as a continuous $\phi^6$ field theory. The authors demonstrate that normalizing flows are powerful generative samplers capable of accurately mapping out the phase diagram across various transition types, including first-order coexistence regions. This provides a modern, data-driven approach to studying classical critical phenomena.
main_problem: The study investigates phase transitions in the Blume-Capel model by mapping it to a continuous $\phi^6$ field theory to test advanced sampling techniques.
main_result: Normalizing flow samplers are shown to be effective across the entire phase diagram, including challenging first-order transition regions, achieving accuracy comparable to traditional Monte Carlo methods.
method: The authors employ Monte Carlo simulations combined with normalizing flows, a generative model, to sample the complex probability distributions associated with the $\phi^6$ lattice field theory.
model_or_system: The system is based on the Blume-Capel model, generalized to a continuous spin $\phi^6$ theory. The Hamiltonian involves nearest-neighbor interactions and higher-order potential terms ($\alpha \sum \phi_i^2 (\phi_i^2 - 1)^2 + \delta \sum \phi_i^2$).
key_observables: Phase diagrams in the crystal-field-temperature plane, critical temperature ($T_c$), and the tricritical point coordinates.
important_parameters: Exchange constant ($J$), crystal field ($\Delta$ or $\delta$), and potential coefficients ($\alpha, \lambda$).
main_assumptions: The soft-spin $\phi^6$ model provides a controlled testbed for studying transitions, and the flow model is assumed to accurately represent the target distribution.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate phase diagrams (e.g., $\phi^6$ theory dependence on $\delta$ and $\alpha$) and show the convergence of the soft-spin tricritical point to the discrete Blume-Capel limit.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by defining the physical models ($\phi^4$ and $\phi^6$), detailing the advanced sampling methods (MC vs. Flow), and presenting results showing the flow model's capability to map out the phase boundaries, especially near tricritical and first-order points.
why_interesting: The application of sophisticated machine learning tools like normalizing flows to map out complex, multi-phase statistical mechanical phase diagrams is highly relevant for understanding critical phenomena in condensed matter systems.

figures.caption: Figure 1. Critical temperatures are found using the crossings of the Binder parameter UL for different linear system sizes L. In this repre- sentative example for the continuous spin variant of the Ising model [Eq. 1] on the square lattice, we chose λ/J = 0.5, resulting in a criti- cal temperature at Tc/J = 3.641.

Figure 2 shows Tc(λ) from a collection of such crossings. Although the un-normalized Tc can exceed the Ising value, the normalized critical temperature is steadily suppressed as λ decreases. This reflects the expected effect of the increased entropy associated with the continuous ϕ field over the dis- crete Ising case, once the trivial ‘length’ effect is removed. Panel (a) of Fig. 3 plots V(ϕ) for four values of λ, illustrating the softening of the potential with the lowering of λ.

Figure 2. Critical temperatures of the continuous spin variant of the Ising model [Eq. 1] on the square lattice as a function of the param- eter λ, which tunes the amount the degrees of freedom deviate from their discrete values ±1. The limit of large λ recovers the Onsager value Tc/J = 2.269. The red circles are Tc/J while the black trian- gles are normalized by ⟨ϕ2⟩. The value of Tc at the smallest λ/J = 0.5 corresponds to the Binder crossing of Fig. 1. Where error bars aren’t visible they lie inside of the point markers.

Figure 3. (a) The potential V(ϕ) for four values of λ in Eq. 1, the soft-spin variant of the Ising model. With increasing λ the wells at ϕ = ±1 become deeper. (b) shows the potential of Eq. 3, the soft-spin variant of the Blume–Capel model, for fixed vacancy potential δ = 1 and varying α, the parameter which tends to confine ϕ to ϕ = 0, ±1. (c) shows fixed α = 16 at several δ. Increasing δ favors vacancies (ϕ = 0). In both (b) and (c), the lower curvature of the ϕ = 0 well relative to the ϕ = ±1 wells is evident. This blurs the mapping to the Blume–Capel limit. See text.

Figure 5. Convergence of the position of the soft-spin tricritical point Tt/J (panel (a)) and ∆t/J (panel (b)) to the discrete Blume–Capel (BC) limits. Error bars are smaller than the markers of the zoomed out plots and are only displayed in the inset. Literature value is from [38].
